newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel expected to cut rates 0.3-0.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel expected to cut rates 0.3-0.5 pct.

text.p: The Bank of Israel is expected to announce an interest rate cut of 0.3 to 0.5 percentage point from a rate of 14.7 percent, analysts said on Monday.
The Bank of Israel is scheduled to announce its February monetary programme at 1430 GMT today.

"My forecast was previously for an 0.3 point decrease based on the consumer price index," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist for Solid Financial Markets. "Now part of me is leaning towards 0.5 point because of the economic indicators released in recent days."
Katz cited the drop in the "S" index of economic performance for November and December, lower industrial production and weak trade figures.
"The whole trend in interest rates is now more downward than previously expected," he said. "You're now looking at negative growth, not just a slowdown."

Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel also faces exchange rate pressures. The shekel has been strong and its currency-basket rate has been near the bottom of the trading band for more than a week, which has forced the Bank of Israel to intervene heavily in the local forex market and inject an estimated $500 million of liquidity into the economy.
Eli Nahum, head of research at Zannex Securities, said the market was also looking for a cut of 0.3 to 0.5 point.

But he and other analysts said the market is focused less on interest rates than on the unfolding government crisis, declining share prices on Wall Street and concerns that the market is overbought after a nearly uninterrupted rise in share prices since the start of November.

Worries about an overbought situation were alleviated by a 3.61 percent plunge in the Mishtanim index of top 100 shares on Sunday. Today the index was up 1.22 percent to 234.75 points in midday trading.
The government crisis, however, may continue to shadow the market, Nahum said.
The crisis stems from allegations of high-level corruption in the appointment of an attorney-general earlier this month. On Sunday, Israeli police launched an investigation into the matter.
Nahum said the affair has sparked worries that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government could fall.
"I personally think that (is the reason for the market's nervousness), but a lot of players don't," he said. "Really, the market was looking for a reason to take profits."
He said the market might be driven by interest rates if the central bank opted to hold rates or to cut them by more than 0.5 point.
